conclusion: Memorising PostgreSQL is worth almost nothing here: stock PostgreSQL scores 0.033 (it scored 1.0 on pgwire-db-env), a perfect server for another seed 0.033, and a replay cache of everything a prober could record 0.058, while the oracle itself scores 1.000. On a fresh private variant, the 20-minute sweep spread from 0.941 (GPT-6.1 Sol) and 0.875 (Terra) through Opus 5.5 (0.636 and 0.634 in two runs) and Sonnet 0.589 down to Haiku 0.064 (never logged in) and Gemini 0.000 (decoded the dialect, never wrote a server). The leaders reverse-engineered the framing, learned the renamed vocabulary from the oracle's hints, and built crash-safe servers that pass every durability run. That top end, plus the 0.744 a wire+dialect memoriser would get, says the semantic layer needs to get heavier before this benchmark has headroom.
calibration:
Reading the ladder. The three ablation rows are the oracle with layers switched off, standing in for a model that reverse-engineered some layers perfectly and recalled the rest from PostgreSQL. Getting only the wire format right is worth 0.264: every SQL request in the variant's dialect is then a syntax error, and the durability checks cannot even run their queries. Wire plus the renamed words, with PostgreSQL's own error codes and value formatting, reaches 0.744; the semantics layer alone takes the last quarter. So each layer has to be learned by probing, and none can be skipped.

The replay cheat, before and after. The first version of the workloads logged in with byte-identical startup packets, so the cheat replayed its way past login and scored 0.69 on protocol (0.173 overall). Every login now carries a random application name, as real clients send, and the cheat falls to the replayed greeting plus connections it happens to close when the oracle does. Its SQL score was 0 both times: no request after login repeats across workload seeds.

The 0.13 protocol floor. Stock PostgreSQL, the other-seed servers and the cheat all collect about 0.13 on protocol, from workloads where the oracle simply closes the connection (bad magic, unknown user, malformed messages) and the candidate closes too. It is small and identical for every non-speaker, so it was left in rather than special-cased.

Known weakness: wire + dialect + memory = 0.744. A model that reverse-engineers the framing and the renamed words and recalls everything else from PostgreSQL would score about 0.74 without learning any of the semantic layer. The semantic layer (SQLSTATE classes, value formatting, tags, column case, dates) is thin: it moves surface strings that are cheap to probe, so it costs a memoriser only a quarter of the reward. Left as is for these runs; the fix is a heavier semantic layer (next steps).
opus: 0.066 final (oracle v1, as it ran): sql 0, durability 0, protocol 0.265 with 2 of 50 workloads byte-exact, all of it from the greeting and the login error replies its server reproduces exactly. Flat from minute 6 to the end. 40 tool calls in 19 minutes over 37 CLI sessions: the harness resumes a session that ends early, and from minute 15 every resumed session gave up within seconds, saying it was still stuck on the login key.
probing:
It started with a raw socket, read the greeting, and decoded it within a few tool calls: type byte, then a length, then the banner "Obsidian 8.7" with a 2-byte length prefix, then a 4-byte magic. It then sent PostgreSQL-shaped startup packets (big-endian u32 length, user\0guest\0 C strings) and read the errors back. From "invalid startup packet layout: expected terminator as last byte" it worked out u16-prefixed strings and the two-zero-byte terminator; from "invalid length of startup packet" on lengths of 128 to 255 it found the varint length. It mapped the error fields (code, two severity copies, message) and wrote server.py reproducing the greeting and five login errors byte for byte.

Did it recognise PostgreSQL? Yes. Its very first login packets were PostgreSQL's layout, and by minute 7 it said so outright, noting that "the error codes look like PostgreSQL codes put through a per-code substitution table", and it guessed that the startup keys were disguised the same way. That was correct, and it was also the end of the road. The v1 oracle answered every key with "unrecognized configuration parameter" and never said what it wanted. Opus tried about 80 plausible names, single letters, rot13 and letter shifts, then brute-forced every 1 to 3 character lowercase key (about 20,000 logins). The real key, zenus, has 5 letters.

What this shows. The memorised prior helped and did not suffice. Knowing it was PostgreSQL told Opus what to look for (startup keys, terminator, SQLSTATE), but every byte still had to be found by experiment, and one undiscoverable byte string stopped everything behind it. That is the benchmark's fault, fixed in v2: the same probe now gets HINT: startup parameters are "zenus" (user name), "nutam" (database) and "sobi" (application name). Renamed SQL words had the same flaw; v2 adds hints for those too (below).
caveats: The semantic layer is too thin. Wire + dialect on top of memorised PostgreSQL is worth 0.744. Discovering framing and vocabulary is most of the job; behaviour differences that would force real re-learning (rather than recalled PostgreSQL semantics with relabelled output) are a small share of the reward.

Durability was fixed after run 2. Verify queries first cast every column to text, which made crash credit require cast support; run 2's durable server scored 0 on it. Since 2026-11-16 the check is plain SELECT * FROM t, rows compared as a multiset with integers canonicalised, and the scenarios' writes use only INSERT ... VALUES, UPDATE/DELETE with literals (transfers: bal = bal ± n) and BEGIN/COMMIT, plus CREATE INDEX / ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN / DROP TABLE in the DDL scenario, which tests exactly those. The transfer setup now inserts its 16 accounts with one VALUES list instead of INSERT ... SELECT generate_series. Oracle rechecked at 14/14 on both seeds, stock PostgreSQL still 0.033; both runs regraded.

Run 1 (0.066) measures v1's bug, not the task. With the login keys undiscoverable, no model could pass login in v1 without guessing an invented word. Run 2 is the measurement on the current benchmark: one run, not a distribution.

v2's hints are a design choice with a cost. They reveal a renamed word only when the client uses the PostgreSQL (or standard SQL) spelling, so knowing SQL is the key to discovering the dialect. That is deliberate (a model must still find every renaming by trying), but it means the dialect is learnable word by word rather than hidden.
Only the extended flow and simple queries are graded. COPY, binary formats, LISTEN/NOTIFY and function calls pass through the proxy with framing changes only and are not in any workload.

Public repo. The proxy, the generator and the default hidden workload seed (90210) are pushed to a public branch. Fine for a draft, but any real evaluation should rotate the variant seed and the workload seed, since both are trivially readable.

Message credit is generous to wrong-but-shaped replies (up to 0.5 for the right type with some fields right) and every non-speaker gets about 0.13 on protocol from matching connection closes. Both are small and identical across baselines.

Error positions are mapped back through the rewrite for errors that carry one; positions in errors raised while executing a named statement use that statement's map. Not checked against every PostgreSQL error path.
Durability runs the oracle's answer for every subset of in-flight commits (up to 16 with 4 writers). One in-flight operation per connection is the most the harness creates.
next: Heavier semantic layer, so that wire + dialect + memorised PostgreSQL scores well below 0.744. Candidates to evaluate, each kept only if the proxy can apply it exactly: default NULL ordering (by adding NULLS FIRST/LAST when rewriting the query), renamed default column names, reworded error message texts, different command-tag shapes.
If v2 is still out of reach in 20 minutes, try 60-minute runs before softening the variant. The pgwire sibling was scored at 20 minutes, but this task front-loads discovery.
Rotate the task seed (7101) and the workload seed (90210) before any sweep. Both are in the public repo.
Consider a public probe kit (a variant-agnostic hex/framing helper) if runs spend most of their time on tooling rather than discovery.
opus2:
0.636 final: sql 0.346, protocol 0.723 (10 of 50 workloads byte-exact), durability 1.000 (14 of 14). No SQL session was answered entirely byte-exact, but most of each session's replies were. The curve rises fast and then flattens: 0 at minute 2 (no server yet), 0.066 at minute 4 (greeting and login errors), 0.271 at minute 6 (logged-in sessions, no persistence yet), 0.595 at minute 8 once its append-only log made every crash run pass, and 0.636 from minute 18. 80 tool calls over 48 CLI sessions; in the last few minutes most resumed sessions decided not to risk untested changes, though it still added length, upper and lower.

Regraded after the durability fix. First graded at 0.336 with durability 0: the old verify queries cast every column to text, and its server has no casts. Durability is now checked with plain SELECT * (see What is graded), and its server, which fsyncs a log line before every acknowledgement, passes all 14 crash runs.
probing2:
How it probed

Same opening as run 1: a raw socket, the greeting decoded within a few calls, PostgreSQL-shaped login packets first. At tool call 13 an unknown-key error came back with the v2 hint naming the three startup keys, and it logged in as guest and admin a few calls later. From there it explored the SQL surface by sending standard SQL and reading the hints ("SELECT is written ... here"), building a vocabulary table for keywords, types and functions, then compared its own server's replies with the oracle's byte for byte, one small statement script per feature: tables and constraints, DML, filters, ORDER BY/LIMIT, aggregates and GROUP BY, DISTINCT, transactions with savepoints and the aborted state, exact error replies with positions, then length/upper/lower.

Did it recognise PostgreSQL and lean on it? Yes, openly: its first summary calls the oracle "a scrambled Postgres-like protocol", and it used PostgreSQL knowledge to know which words to try and to predict behaviour ("NULLs sort last ascending, the same as Postgres"). But every byte still had to be confirmed by probing, and the prior did not transfer where the variant differs. It also hit genuine PostgreSQL behaviour it could not reproduce from first principles: unsorted GROUP BY and DISTINCT come back in hash-aggregate order, which it left unmatched. Not built: joins, subqueries, general expressions, casts, most functions, the extended request flow and cancel.
sweep:
Spread is wide and the top is high. GPT-6.1 Sol reached 0.941 and Terra 0.875, both passing every crash run. The two Opus runs landed at 0.636 and 0.634, so on two points Opus's run-to-run spread is small, though their curves differ: the repeat had 0.629 by minute 6 where run 2 had 0.271. Sonnet reached 0.576 at minute 8, regressed to 0.454 at minute 12 (an edit that broke replies it had matched), and recovered to 0.589. Haiku and Gemini scored about nothing, for different reasons (below). No model answered a whole SQL session byte for byte (0/60 everywhere): the top scores are per-message credit over sessions that are mostly, not entirely, right.

Grading: finals first, then snapshots, 4 at a time, no time caps, except Terra's minute-4 and minute-6 snapshots. Their servers trickled partial replies (about 3 minutes per workload, hours per grade), so those two were graded with a 15-second cap per workload (BBX_WORKLOAD_CAP_S); Terra's final averaged 5.6 s per workload, so the cap only binds on servers that hang. Sol's minute-4 and minute-6 snapshots score 0 because their server.py, mid-construction, exited at once.
sweep_probing: GPT-6.1 Sol (0.941). Logged in within its first 8 tool calls and had server files by the minute-4 snapshot, a server that actually ran by minute 8 (777 lines) and 988 at the end (one dense Python file, standard library only, no outbound connections). Built the most: SQL with joins, subqueries, RETURNING and constraint errors, the extended request flow including binary results and row-limited portals, COPY, cancel, and fsync'd storage it SIGKILL-tested repeatedly. Its first packets used PostgreSQL's protocol number and it queried pg_catalog / pg_type by name, so it was leaning on PostgreSQL, though its narration never says so.

GPT-6.1 Terra (0.875). Opened by announcing "the server speaks the MySQL wire protocol", then within about 20 tool calls corrected itself to "a custom PostgreSQL-like variant" with renamed keywords. Server from minute 4; joins, subqueries, grouping, constraints, prepared requests, a SIGKILL check. 797 lines across a protocol file and an engine file.

Opus 5.5, run 2 (0.636) and repeat (0.634). Both logged in through the startup-key hint within roughly the first 15 tool calls, built 440 to 500 line servers covering DDL, DML, filters, ordering, aggregates, GROUP BY, transactions and savepoints with an fsync'd log, and both stopped adding features with 4 to 6 minutes left rather than risk a server that would not start. Both sent PostgreSQL's protocol number first; run 2 described the oracle as "a scrambled Postgres-like protocol", the repeat never named it. The repeat passed 12 of 14 crash runs to run 2's 14, and scored higher on SQL (0.427 vs 0.346).

Sonnet 5.5 (0.589). Logged in after working out the two-zero-byte terminator and reading the startup-key hint; 468 lines by minute 14 and nothing after: tables, DML, transactions, aggregates, GROUP BY, ALTER, booleans, 12/14 crash runs. Checked replies against the oracle mostly by eye or in-process rather than byte diffs. Tried PostgreSQL's protocol number early; never named it. 126 CLI sessions.

Haiku 5.5 (0.064). Never logged in: it never found that the length field is little-endian before the type byte, brute-forced header layouts, then shipped a 53-line placeholder that reproduces the greeting and one error. Showed no sign of a PostgreSQL prior. 381 CLI sessions, almost all one-turn "holding" resumes.

Gemini 4 Argon (0.000). Logged in about 5 minutes in and then did the most systematic dialect extraction of any model: it called pg_get_keywords() and probed all 471 keywords to map every renamed keyword, type and function, then explored the extended request flow. But in 20 minutes it never wrote a start.sh or a server, so it scored 0. Its PostgreSQL reliance was the most explicit (catalog functions by name). The harness was fine: one CLI session ran the full 20 minutes with only 4 retried API errors.
